cells.tense: Here, at the table, the shape of what has finished is visible and can be left finished.
cells.act: notice what is newly here, right now
cells.ask: Find the edge of something that has run its course. Then look at what's around you now that wasn't there at the start. Say nothing yet. Nothing has to follow unless you want it to.
cells.core:
Standing where the whole pattern shows itself, you can find the edge of a thing without flinching from it. You tell what's done from what's only tired, and you catch that the person beside you reads slightly new each time. That's the balance: a chapter can close and the room stays open. The meeting that ended when it should, the friendship that finished kindly — those are yours to let be finished, no reopening and no last word.

What it asks of you here is plainer than it sounds. Some things have genuinely reached their end and are being carried out of habit. Saying so to yourself costs nothing and changes nothing yet. It just shows you where here is. What's arriving next doesn't need a scene made for it. It needs you near the door, hearing the knock.
cells.sheetLine: A thing can finish without being called a failure.
cells.verb: Completing what is ready and opening the door to the next

cells.tense: Soon there won't be time to get this right, so endings are being declared before they happen.
cells.act: open the door to the next thing on time, not early
cells.ask: When something feels finished ahead of its hour, hold. Give it a day before you say it's over. If it's truly done, it will still be done tomorrow.
cells.core:
You can see the whole arc of a thing from inside it. That's the gift. But lately it has sped up: you name the ending while the story is mid-scene, close the account before the last payment lands. Someone is still saying the sentence and you've understood how it finishes. It isn't cruelty. It's the loose end you can't stand — the thing that might keep going without you.

What that costs: nobody gets to arrive. Every threshold gets crossed before anyone touches it. The answer isn't to see less; it's to let what you see lag behind what's happening by a beat. The ending will keep. The middle is the part you can't get back, and the middle is where the other person lives.

cells.tense: A door closed and you're still standing at it, calling it unfinished.
cells.act: take the turning as it comes
cells.ask: Take the turning you keep postponing. A half-step counts. Set the new date, clear the old shelf, sit with the person who's actually here. Nothing is required after that.
cells.core:
The pattern is visible to you; it's the closing that has gone quiet. You can describe the arc of the thing perfectly — and you won't put the last mark on it. There's one more version to look for, one more door that might open, one more person who might finally answer. The search has become its own room. You live in it.

What's true: a cycle left open takes your whole attention and gives nothing back. It doesn't matter whether the story ended well. It ended. Standing at the door of a finished room isn't fidelity, it's stasis. Notice what has actually turned; you'll know by what no longer asks anything of you. Then turn. Even a half-step. Even unsure. Especially then.
cells.sheetLine: A finished thing stays open because closing it would be real.

cells.tense: The pen is down and the room is quiet, and you haven't looked at what you already wrote.
cells.act: put it down and leave your hands empty a while
cells.ask: Name a grip you're still holding — a version of the story, a plan, a grudge. Set it down and keep your hands open. Do the work; stop steering the outcome. See what happens without you.
cells.core:
Some part of you has already completed the pattern and simply hasn't been told. You describe the chapter in present tense while the actual room has changed, the people have moved, the season is gone. The whole shape gets seen — you say it beautifully — but you don't recognize that you're standing at the far end of it. It isn't denial. The completion happened and you missed that it happened, so something keeps re-walking the hall to check the lights.

The gift here is odd: releasing feels like loss, but what you'd release has already released you. Put down the story about what's unresolved. Tell the pattern to one person, or leave it on a page. Saying the whole thing is the last act that makes it real.
